newsitem.title: FRANCE: Mass protest as French far right opens congress.
newsitem.headline: Mass protest as French far right opens congress.

text.p: Tens of thousands of protesters marched through Strasbourg on Saturday as France's far-right National Front, calling voters of mainstream parties cuckolds, met to map strategy for next year's general election.

Row upon row of riot police, and hundreds of the party's own burly security guards, sealed off the congress building in the reluctant eastern host city as leader Jean-Marie Le Pen arrived to tell delegates of his confidence in an election breakthrough.

"Let us continue on our great ascent, to the beat of the drums of those who believe they are fighting us," the Front's General Secretary Bruno Gollnisch said in the opening speech, calling the meeting "the congress of the great alternative".
Strasbourg's Socialist mayor Catherine Trautmann has called in 2,000 police and appealed for calm in the march which drew protesters from across the country, Germany and Switzerland.
An early police estimate said 25,000 took part.

"Those who call themselves our enemies...are calling for help against the National Front -- the German Reds and Greens, all the thugs from across the Rhine, international socialists like their fathers were national socialists," Gollnisch said.
The feisty Le Pen, who won 15 percent of the vote in the 1995 presidential poll, has vowed an assault on the political establishment in the run-up to a March 1998 general election.

"We believe that if the French people still vote for the Socialists or the (ruling Gaullist) RPR, it is their absolute right, as after all cuckolds have the right to be happy with their misfortunes," Gollnisch said.
The Front was buoyed by winning control of Vitrolles in a municipal election last month, the fourth town it controls in southern France after Toulon, Orange and Marignane.

Le Pen and his deputy Bruno Megret rejected charges made in interviews to the daily Le Parisien by Socialist Party leader and Communist chief Robert Hue that the anti-immigrant Front was racist, anti-Semitic, xenophobic and fascist.
"We believe that if the French people knew what we truly think -- and not the caricature provided by our adversaries -- we would have a majority, as in Vitrolles," Le Pen, 68, said.

"Our criterion is not race. Our criterion is nation," he told reporters. He said the congress would add to the Front's statutes a clause saying it is committed to democracy and French nationals whatever their race, origin or creed.
The Front calls for sending immigrants home and giving preference to French nationals for jobs and social benefits.

Protesters poured in on chartered "freedom trains" and buses. Front leaders advised the 2,200 delegates to remain closeted in the congress, warning authorities they would responsible for any violence.
A red flag with a swastika was briefly hoisted on the spire of the towering Gothic cathedral as local officials visited the site of a synagogue burnt down by the Nazis in World War Two.
Representatives of the anti-racist group MRAP laid a wreath at the site of the Struthof Nazi World War Two concentration camp, near Strasbourg, where some 25,000 died.
Giant city hall posters in various languages outside the congress centre proclaimed the motto of the French Republic -- "liberty, equality, fraternity".
Anti-Front protesters, saying they were "mourning democracy", planted black flowers, painted black bands on street signs and blindfolded statues in black.
The Strasbourg march capped a groundswell of opposition to Le Pen which was fuelled by the Front victory in Vitrolles and a hardline government law to curb immigration.

France's first-past-the-post election system has kept the Front out from parliament, but delegates sounded confident it can ride to power on record 12.8 percent unemployment and simmering resentment of North African immigrants and political corruption.
A survey in the weekly Le Point said that the Front would poll 15 percent of the vote, up from 12.5 percent in 1993, but would remain out of parliament if the election was held now.
Politicians disagree on how to counter the Front's rise. The ruling centre-right coalition refused to join the march, arguing it would mainly serve to keep the Front in the public eye.

The congress is to re-elect Le Pen as president, choose a central committee and draft an election platform and campaign strategy. The party's founder, Le Pen is unopposed and has refused to discuss a successor. 291542 GMT mar 97
